Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 1) Total body water in a healthy adult male constitutes approximately:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Total body water averages about 60% of body weight in adult males and is relatively lower in females due to higher body fat.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 2) The largest fluid compartment in the body is:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Approximately two-thirds of total body water is contained within cells.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 3) Intracellular fluid accounts for approximately what proportion of total body water?
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Intracellular fluid is the largest fluid compartment, containing about two-thirds of total body water.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 4) The principal cation of the extracellular fluid is:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Sodium is the major extracellular cation and plays a key role in maintaining extracellular osmolality.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 5) The principal cation of the intracellular fluid is:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Potassium is the predominant intracellular cation and is essential for normal cellular function.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 6) The principal anion of the extracellular fluid is:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Chloride is the major extracellular anion and helps maintain electrical neutrality.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 7) The principal intracellular anion is:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Phosphate and proteins are the major intracellular anions.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 8) Which electrolyte is the major determinant of extracellular fluid osmolality?
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Plasma osmolality depends primarily on sodium concentration and its accompanying anions.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 9) Normal plasma osmolality is approximately:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Normal plasma osmolality ranges between 275 and 295 mOsm/kg.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 10) The principal hormone regulating water reabsorption in the kidney is:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Antidiuretic hormone increases water reabsorption in the collecting ducts.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 11) ADH is synthesized in the:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: ADH is synthesized in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 12) Aldosterone primarily increases renal reabsorption of:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Aldosterone promotes sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion in the distal nephron.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 13) The major stimulus for aldosterone secretion is:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Increased serum potassium is a potent direct stimulus for aldosterone secretion.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 14) The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system is activated primarily by:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Decreased renal blood flow stimulates renin release, activating the RAAS.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 15) Which electrolyte abnormality is most likely to produce muscle weakness and cardiac arrhythmias?
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Potassium is essential for normal neuromuscular and cardiac electrical activity.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 16) The normal serum sodium concentration is approximately:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Serum sodium is tightly regulated within this normal physiological range.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 17) The normal serum potassium concentration is approximately:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Normal potassium concentration is maintained within a narrow range to preserve cardiac function.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 18) Which electrolyte is mainly responsible for maintaining the resting membrane potential?
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: The potassium gradient across the cell membrane is the major determinant of resting membrane potential.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 19) A patient with prolonged vomiting is most likely to develop:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Gastric fluid contains a large amount of hydrochloric acid; prolonged vomiting causes chloride depletion.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 20) The principal buffer system in extracellular fluid is:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: The bicarbonate-carbonic acid system is the major extracellular buffer maintaining blood pH.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 21) Normal arterial blood pH is:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Normal arterial blood pH is maintained within this narrow range by buffer systems, lungs and kidneys.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 22) The normal arterial PCO₂ is approximately:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Normal arterial carbon dioxide tension is about 40 mmHg.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 23) The normal plasma bicarbonate concentration is approximately:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Plasma bicarbonate normally ranges from about 22–26 mmol/L.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 24) Respiratory acidosis is primarily caused by:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Hypoventilation leads to carbon dioxide retention, increasing carbonic acid and lowering blood pH.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 25) A patient with severe diarrhea develops metabolic acidosis. The primary mechanism is excessive loss of:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Intestinal secretions contain bicarbonate; excessive loss in diarrhea produces a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 26) The primary compensatory response to metabolic acidosis is:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Hyperventilation lowers PaCO₂, helping to raise blood pH and partially compensate for metabolic acidosis.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 27) Respiratory alkalosis is most commonly caused by:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Excessive loss of carbon dioxide due to hyperventilation raises blood pH, resulting in respiratory alkalosis.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 28) Metabolic alkalosis is commonly associated with:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Vomiting causes excessive loss of hydrochloric acid, increasing plasma bicarbonate concentration.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 29) Which organ provides the fastest compensation for metabolic acid-base disorders?
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Respiratory compensation occurs within minutes by altering alveolar ventilation.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 30) Which organ is primarily responsible for long-term regulation of acid-base balance?
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: The kidneys regulate acid-base balance by excreting hydrogen ions and regenerating bicarbonate.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 31) The normal anion gap is approximately:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: The normal anion gap is approximately 8–12 mmol/L when potassium is excluded.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 32) Which of the following commonly causes a high anion gap metabolic acidosis?
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Accumulation of ketoacids increases the anion gap and produces metabolic acidosis.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 33) Which condition typically causes a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis?
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Bicarbonate loss in diarrhea is balanced by increased chloride, producing hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 34) The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation describes the relationship between blood pH and:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Blood pH depends on the ratio of bicarbonate concentration to dissolved carbon dioxide.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 35) The principal intracellular buffer is:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: The phosphate buffer system is particularly important inside cells and in renal tubular fluid.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 36) Hemoglobin functions physiologically as an important:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Hemoglobin buffers hydrogen ions generated during carbon dioxide transport.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 37) The kidneys compensate for respiratory acidosis by:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Renal compensation conserves bicarbonate and increases hydrogen ion excretion.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 38) Which electrolyte disturbance is most commonly associated with metabolic alkalosis?
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Potassium depletion frequently accompanies metabolic alkalosis, especially following vomiting or diuretic therapy.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 39) Tetany is most likely to occur in:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Alkalosis increases calcium binding to albumin, lowering ionized calcium and causing tetany.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 40) Which electrolyte abnormality produces peaked T waves on ECG?
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Hyperkalemia classically causes tall peaked T waves and may progress to life-threatening arrhythmias.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 41) Flattened T waves and prominent U waves are characteristic of:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Hypokalemia delays ventricular repolarization, producing flattened T waves and U waves.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 42) Which electrolyte disturbance is most likely to cause muscle weakness, constipation and polyuria?
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Hypercalcemia reduces neuromuscular excitability and impairs renal concentrating ability.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 43) The most common symptom of acute hyponatremia is:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Cerebral edema caused by acute hyponatremia produces neurological symptoms.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 44) Hypernatremia primarily results in:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Increased extracellular osmolality draws water out of cells, causing cellular shrinkage.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 45) A patient with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus develops excessive thirst because increased plasma osmolality stimulates:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Increased plasma osmolality activates hypothalamic osmoreceptors, stimulating both thirst and ADH secretion.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 46) Which electrolyte is essential for normal neuromuscular transmission and blood coagulation?
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Calcium plays a critical role in muscle contraction, neurotransmitter release and coagulation.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 47) A patient with chronic kidney disease is most likely to develop:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Reduced renal acid excretion leads to retention of hydrogen ions and metabolic acidosis.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 48) Which electrolyte abnormality commonly accompanies diabetic ketoacidosis before treatment?
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Although total body potassium is depleted, serum potassium is often elevated before insulin therapy due to extracellular potassium shift.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 49) A patient develops carpopedal spasm after thyroid surgery. The most likely electrolyte disturbance is:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Accidental parathyroid injury can lead to hypocalcemia, causing tetany and carpopedal spasm.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 50) An anxious young woman is breathing rapidly. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.52, PaCO₂ 28 mmHg and HCO₃⁻ 24 mmol/L. The most likely diagnosis is:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Elevated pH with low PaCO₂ and normal bicarbonate indicates acute respiratory alkalosis due to hyperventilation.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 51) The major intracellular buffer system is:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: The phosphate buffer system is the principal intracellular buffer and also contributes significantly to buffering in renal tubular fluid.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 52) The major extracellular buffer system is:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: The bicarbonate-carbonic acid buffer is the primary extracellular buffer maintaining blood pH.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 53) Which electrolyte is the most abundant intracellular cation?
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Potassium is the predominant intracellular cation and is essential for maintaining membrane potential.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 54) Which electrolyte is the most abundant extracellular cation?
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Sodium is the principal extracellular cation and largely determines extracellular fluid volume.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 55) The normal arterial blood pH is maintained by the combined action of:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Acid-base homeostasis depends on chemical buffers, respiratory regulation of CO₂, and renal control of bicarbonate and hydrogen ion excretion.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 56) The principal stimulus for ADH secretion is:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect increased plasma osmolality and stimulate ADH release.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 57) A patient with diabetes insipidus is most likely to present with:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Deficiency or resistance to ADH results in excessive dilute urine and increased thirst.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 58) Which electrolyte abnormality is most commonly associated with diabetes insipidus if water intake is inadequate?
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Excessive free water loss without adequate replacement raises serum sodium concentration.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 59) Which condition is most likely to produce dilutional hyponatremia?
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Excess ADH causes water retention, leading to dilution of serum sodium.

Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.question: 60) A patient with serum sodium of 118 mmol/L develops confusion and seizures. The most likely diagnosis is:
Body Fluid, Electrolytes & Acid–Base Bal.exp: Severe hyponatremia causes cerebral edema, leading to neurological manifestations such as confusion, seizures and coma.
